many reasons. the most obvious of which is that rocket engines sit on the razor's edge between incredibly sophisticated transportation technology and a bomb. the science is to balance on that edge.
Let me point you here, read up on all the variables. Then trust a 100 million $ satellite on any thing less engineered. Solid fuel rocket engines are a different monster all together.

(A) Rockets are under two pressures: performance and weight. They need to perform to the absolute MAX with every possible gram shaved away. That's tough.

(B) Rockets are basically a controlled explosion. When something goes wrong, it doesn't fizzle or shut down. It goes BOOM.

Does it differ from a car? An aerodynamic box powered by continuous explosions. Perhaps ita very similar but the scale (required to escape the atmosphere) amplifies possible defects that are undetectable otherwise.

It's all about scale. A bridge, much like a rocket, is fundamentally simple. You can build a bridge out of tooth picks and glue that's suitable for a mouse, but ramp the size up to 600' long and 30' wide and have to hold thousands of pounds to ensure the safety of travelers and other factors that crop up when you increase the scale such as natural events like tornadoes and hurricanes and everything gets a good deal more complicated.

Rocket engines must optimize mass over incredible extremes of performance. They require cutting-edge materials and fabrication processes and it has traditionally taken a very long time and a lot of money to develop a reliable rocket engine, usually as a part of a whole launch system rather than an individual interchangeable part. Around 5-10 years and half a billion dollars. They may seem simple but they are simple in the way that a PC or smartphone is--simplicity resulting from extreme sophistication in engineering. Only very recently has there emerged a concept of 'open source' development and knowledge sharing in aerospace since its association with the military has imposed great secrecy on everything. So there's no 'industrial ecology' in aerospace the way there is in electronics. Everything aerospace companies make are like Faberge Eggs. What they produce is very sophisticated, but the way they go about its development is rather primitive.

Commercial interests would much rather exploit what governments and their taxpayers have already paid for then spend their own money. So most commercial rockets in existence have derived from rockets originally created by/for the military on the taxpayer's dime. (most of them originally ICBMs) And it's down to chance whether or not these things can be commercially repurposed, but because most rockets are physically simple--basically just tubes of different scales--they do tend to be easily repurposed. Oddly, this has not been the case with rockets developed by/for the space agencies because they've tended to be too specialized or just not economically rational. For instance, commercial space developers could have readily created their own Space Shuttles but never did because the system was economically unsustainable. A manned cargo vehicle never made sense outside the logic of NASA.

In the case of the Russian RD-180 engine, a different history of development led to families of engines in differrent countries with differrent characteristics that have proven expensive to reproduce starting from scratch. The RD-180 originated with the Zenit launch system which was originally an ICBM intended to be launched in the water off the back of ships. This is a class of rocket the US once explored as well but here political competition between the Navy and the Air Force resulted in the Air Force coming to dominate nuclear weapons deployment and so this class of rocket was abandoned here but persisted in Russia for some time. More-or-less by chance, the Zenit system proved quite versatile as a smaller commercial launch platform as scales of satellites shrank (the opposite of what was long expected) and has been used in many variations. The SeaLaunch program also used the Zenit rocket. So it's really just a side effect of history that Russia happened to have an engine with these performance characteristics and the US didn't, and commercial developers don't want to spend money reinventing from scratch what they can get off-the-shelf--even if that's become geopolitically inconvenient at present.
